issues.description: The entire results section is based on randomly generated dummy data from Qualtrics (N=1000), not actual participant data. All statistical tests, effect sizes, p-values, and conclusions are meaningless artifacts of random number generation. The manuscript presents these results as if they are interpretable findings, including drawing conclusions about hypotheses (e.g., 'no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning') and making comparisons to the original study. This fundamentally undermines the entire paper.
issues.quote: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.description: The procedures section states that 'Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions,' which means participants self-selected into experimental conditions rather than being randomly assigned. This completely undermines the experimental design and makes causal inference impossible due to self-selection bias. The original study used random assignment. This is a fundamental departure that invalidates the between-subjects factorial design.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The design section describes the study as 'a single within-subject design' but the original studies used between-subjects designs, and the analysis (two-way ANOVA with separate cell sizes across conditions) clearly indicates a between-subjects design. The unequal cell sizes across conditions (e.g., 159, 175, 166) also confirm between-subjects assignment. This is a fundamental mislabeling of the experimental design.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.subcategory: Abstract conclusions drawn from dummy data
issues.description: The abstract presents substantive conclusions about the hypotheses based on randomly generated data, stating 'no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning' and that 'Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation.' These conclusions are entirely meaningless since they are derived from random data, yet they are presented as actual findings.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: Absence of real donation as DV
issues.description: The original study had participants donate real money ($5 they had earned), whereas this replication uses imaginary/hypothetical donation. This is a major deviation that undermines construct validity, as hypothetical and real donation decisions involve different psychological processes. Hypothetical donations are known to be inflated and less sensitive to experimental manipulations. This deviation is acknowledged but its implications for replication validity are not discussed.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The original study gave participants $5 from a prior survey, creating an endowment that participants could then donate. The replication omits this entirely, meaning participants have no endowment to donate from. This changes the psychological framing from donating 'found money' to purely hypothetical donation, which is a significant methodological deviation that could affect the identifiable victim effect.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.subcategory: Implausible age statistics from dummy data
issues.description: The dummy data reports a mean age of 67.80 with SD=30.10 and an age range of 18-120. An age of 120 is biologically implausible, and the mean age of ~68 is far too high for any typical participant sample (MTurk or otherwise). While this is acknowledged as dummy data, it demonstrates that the random data generation was not constrained to realistic parameters, raising concerns about whether any of the dummy analyses are informative about what the actual results pipeline will produce.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males)

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc means inconsistent with descriptive statistics table
issues.description: In the results text interpreting Table 10, the authors report that participants facing statistical victims donated more (M=2.54, SD=1.76) than those facing identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67). However, Table 7 shows different values: identifiable victim conditions have means of 2.58 and 2.50, and statistical victim conditions have means of 2.46 and 2.01. The marginal means reported in the text (2.54 and 2.24) do not match any straightforward calculation from Table 7, and the direction of the effect (statistical > identifiable) contradicts the identifiable victim effect hypothesis.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)

issues.description: The post-hoc test in Table 10 shows that statistical victims received MORE donations than identifiable victims (the t-value is negative for Identifiable VS Statistical, and the text confirms this direction). This is the opposite of the identifiable victim effect (Hypothesis 1 predicts people donate MORE to identifiable victims). Yet this contradiction is not explicitly flagged or discussed in the results section.
issues.quote: participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)

issues.description: The dependent variable has been changed from actual monetary donation (behavioral measure) to a hypothetical donation intention (self-report measure). This represents a construct validity problem because the identifiable victim effect is theorized to operate through affective mechanisms that influence actual behavior. Hypothetical measures are subject to social desirability bias and may not capture the same psychological processes. The replication classification as 'close to very close' may be overstated given this change.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The manuscript references a power analysis in the supplementary materials but does not report the target sample size, the effect size used for the power calculation, the desired power level, or how the N=1000 was determined. The text says 'The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power' but provides no specifics in the main manuscript.
issues.quote: The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary

issues.description: The manuscript mentions excluding participants with prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect and those who failed attention checks, but does not specify the attention check items, the criteria for determining prior knowledge, or how many participants were excluded (or will be excluded) based on these criteria.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The authors merged Studies 1 and 3 into a single experiment and applied the intervention (learning about the identifiable victim effect) to the joint condition, which was not done in the original Study 3. This changes the design substantially: in the original, the joint condition was an implicit manipulation without explicit teaching. Adding the explicit intervention to the joint condition confounds the implicit and explicit debiasing mechanisms, making it impossible to cleanly test Hypothesis 4 about implicit debiasing.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect, indicated in the imaginary donation to corresponding victims across conditions. The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition

issues.subcategory: Sample and setting differences not adequately addressed
issues.description: The original study used university students in a laboratory setting in Pennsylvania, while the replication uses MTurk workers online. The manuscript acknowledges this as a deviation but does not discuss how the different sample characteristics (age, motivation, attention, cultural context) and setting (online vs. lab) might affect the identifiable victim effect or the effectiveness of the deliberative thinking manipulation.
issues.quote: MTurk workers as participants We will recruit participants on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study recruited participants sitting inside the school centre of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: The replication is classified as 'close to very close' despite multiple substantial deviations: hypothetical instead of real donations, no endowment/pre-survey compensation, online instead of lab setting, different participant population, merging two studies into one, adding intervention to the joint condition, and different DV stimuli. Several of these changes are classified as 'Different' in the authors' own Table 6. This classification appears overly generous.
issues.quote: Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.subcategory: Residual df inconsistent with reported sample sizes
issues.description: Table 9 reports residual df = 994 for the replication. With a 2×3 design and 6 cells, the residual df should be N - 6 = 1000 - 6 = 994, which is consistent. However, the total of cell sizes in Table 7 is 159+175+166+175+159+166 = 1000, which would give residual df = 994. This is consistent, but it implies no participants were excluded despite the stated exclusion criteria. This suggests the exclusion criteria were not applied to the dummy data, which is expected but should be noted.
issues.quote: Residual | Original study | 115 | Replication | 994

issues.description: Hypothesis 6 states that 'An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims.' However, the significant post-hoc result (Table 14) shows the difference is between statistical and joint conditions (not identifiable vs. statistical), and the direction shows statistical victims had HIGHER perceived impact (M=3.12) than the joint condition (M=2.85). The identifiable vs. statistical comparison was non-significant. Yet the abstract claims results 'supported the hypothesis.'
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: The manuscript does not provide the specific items or scales used to measure the affective feelings (upsetting, sympathy, touched, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, perceived impact). The response scale, anchors, and exact wording are not reported in the main manuscript, making it impossible to evaluate construct validity or replicate the measures.

issues.subcategory: Missing information on aggregated feelings computation
issues.description: The manuscript mentions 'aggregated feelings' as a composite of segregated feelings but does not report how the aggregation was performed (simple average, sum, weighted), whether reliability was assessed (e.g., Cronbach's alpha), or which specific items were included in the aggregate.
issues.quote: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.description: The analysis plan specifies that post-hoc contrast tests and Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons will only be conducted 'if the interaction effect is significant' or 'if the effect of identifiability and intervention are significant.' This conditional testing strategy introduces analytic flexibility and can inflate Type I error rates, as the decision to conduct further tests depends on the outcome of prior tests.
issues.quote: Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant

issues.description: The manuscript attributes the identifiable victim effect to the 'availability heuristic' (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), but the availability heuristic refers to judging frequency or probability based on ease of recall. The mechanism described (affective reactions to personalized information) is more accurately characterized as the affect heuristic (Slovic et al., 2007) or vividness effects. While Small & Loewenstein (2003) is cited, the theoretical framing conflates distinct cognitive mechanisms.
issues.quote: The "availability heuristic" (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual (Small & Loewenstein, 2003).

issues.description: The manuscript lacks a discussion section entirely. There is no interpretation of findings, no comparison of replication results to original findings using the stated evaluation criteria (Lebel et al., 2019), no discussion of limitations, and no consideration of what the results mean for the identifiable victim effect literature. The evaluation framework (Figure 1) is introduced but never applied to the results.

Table 4 ('Difference and similarities between the original study and replication') has three columns for data but the last two columns appear to contain identical information (both labeled as Qualtrics generated response with the same values). This appears to be a formatting error.
issues.quote: Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.description: There is no mention of a manipulation check to verify that the intervention (learning about the identifiable victim effect) was effective in inducing deliberative thinking. The original study also lacked this, but for a replication attempting to test whether deliberative thinking reduces the identifiable victim effect, confirming that the manipulation worked is important.
The name 'Slovic' is repeatedly misspelled as 'Solvic' in the introduction, creating confusion about which author is being referenced.
issues.quote: Solvic (2007) argued for the drawbacks of the phenomenon

issues.subcategory: Online setting may undermine affective manipulation
issues.description: The shift from a controlled laboratory environment to an online MTurk survey may substantially reduce the effectiveness of the affective manipulation. In the original study, participants physically handled money and signed a charity letter, creating a more vivid and engaging experience. Online participants may be less attentive and less emotionally engaged, which is particularly problematic for a study that relies on affective responses to drive the identifiable victim effect.

issues.subcategory: Effect size confidence interval includes zero despite significant p-value
issues.description: In Table 10, the Identifiable VS Statistical comparison is reported as significant (pBonferroni = .049) with d = 0.076, but the 95% CI for d is [-0.05, 0.20], which includes zero. While this can occur with Bonferroni-adjusted p-values near the threshold, it raises concerns about the robustness of this finding and whether the CI corresponds to the adjusted or unadjusted test.

issues.subcategory: No plan for handling missing data or attrition
issues.description: The manuscript does not describe any plan for handling missing data, incomplete responses, or participant attrition in the actual data collection. Given that this is an online study where dropout rates can be substantial, this is an important omission for the pre-registration.
